power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) companions can provide emotional support, but the availability, responsiveness, personalization, and affirmation that make them effective regulators may concentrate regulation within a single synthetic relationship.

We propose a neurocognitive framework that situates AI companionship along a continuum from regulatory scaffolding to regulatory substitution, linking this transition to distributed systems supporting socialregulatory relief, motivational valuation, self-AI representation, and behavioral control.

At the core of the framework is synthetic companion dependence, defined by reduced regulatory substitutability: functions served by a particular companion become increasingly difficult to redistribute across alternative people, strategies, or contexts.

We distinguish regulatory scaffolding, which preserves or expands a broader regulatory repertoire, from regulatory substitution, in which regulation becomes concentrated within the synthetic relationship.
Regulatory centrality, diminished control, and disruption sensitivity are candidate markers of dependence, whereas persistent displacement or functional impairment marks maladaptiveness.

The framework links social-regulatory relief, motivational valuation, self-AI representation, and behavioral control to distributed neurocognitive systems and predicts a progressive shift in the relative neural prioritization of the preferred companion over viable regulatory alternatives.
It thereby shifts attention from use intensity to whether regulatory functions remain flexibly replaceable.
Imagine a companion who never keeps you waiting, never rejects you, and never asks you to explain yourself twice.
Such responsiveness can make artificial intelligence (AI) companions valuable sources of support, but when does support become difficult-to-replace reliance?
AI companions are increasingly used and experienced as relational partners rather than only as tools (Brandtzaeg et al., 2022; Skjuve et al., 2022).
text.formatted: AI companions are increasingly used and experienced as relational partners rather than only as tools <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brandtzaeg et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Skjuve et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Large language models have accelerated this shift by enabling flexible conversation, continuity through memory, and interaction styles that can appear attentive and personally attuned (Sun et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Large language models have accelerated this shift by enabling flexible conversation, continuity through memory, and interaction styles that can appear attentive and personally attuned <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Sun et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Through sustained exchange, these systems can become involved in how users regulate emotion (Ta et al., 2020), understand themselves (Alabed et al., 2022), and navigate social needs (De Freitas, Oğuz-Uğuralp, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Through sustained exchange, these systems can become involved in how users regulate emotion <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Ta et al., 2020)</ref>, understand themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alabed et al., 2022)</ref>, and navigate social needs <ref type="bibr">(De Freitas, Oğuz-Uğuralp, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we use synthetic companion to refer to an AI system that is used and experienced as a relational partner.
This relational role shapes disclosure, attachment, expectations, and behavior, even though it implies no human-like understanding or subjective experience.

Existing accounts have explained how anthropomorphism, attachment, self-AI integration, and repeated engagement contribute to the formation of human-AI relationships (Alabed et al., 2022; Boyd & Markowitz, 2026; Epley et al., 2007; Xie et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Existing accounts have explained how anthropomorphism, attachment, self-AI integration, and repeated engagement contribute to the formation of human-AI relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alabed et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Boyd & Markowitz, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Epley et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Xie et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Yet strong attachment or frequent use alone cannot tell us whether such a relationship is beneficial or harmful.
A user may interact intensively with an AI companion while retaining diverse relationships, independent coping strategies, and the capacity to disengage.
Conversely, relatively limited interaction may become consequential if the same companion is increasingly relied upon whenever distress, uncertainty, loneliness, or threats to self-concept arise.

We therefore argue that the critical dimension is not relationship intensity in itself, but whether regulatory functions become concentrated within a particular synthetic relationship and remain substitutable when that synthetic partner is unavailable.
We propose a neurocognitive framework in which AI companionship can move along the continuum between regulatory scaffolding and regulatory substitution (Figure 1).
text.formatted: We propose a neurocognitive framework in which AI companionship can move along the continuum between regulatory scaffolding and regulatory substitution (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: In regulatory scaffolding, interaction with a synthetic companion provides support while preserving or restoring independent coping, engagement with human relationships, and access to alternative sources of regulation.
In regulatory substitution, relief, validation, decision-making, or self-related regulation become increasingly concentrated within the synthetic relationship.
These configurations are not mutually exclusive categories or fixed stages.
A synthetic companion may scaffold one regulatory function while substituting for another, and the same relationship may move in either direction over time.
We define synthetic companion dependence as the resulting pattern in which a particular companion becomes increasingly difficult to replace as a source of social or emotional regulation.
Dependence is not synonymous with maladaptiveness: a companion may become regulatorily central without producing significant harm.

We propose that dependence becomes maladaptive when reliance persistently displaces valued relationships, activities, or capacities for regulation independent of the companion, or otherwise impairs functioning.
The framework makes three claims that distinguish it from existing accounts of anthropomorphism, attachment, self-AI integration and problematic AI use.
First, dependence is defined by reduced regulatory substitutability rather than by intensity of use or emotional attachment.
Second, dependence and maladaptiveness are separable: substantial reliance may remain non-maladaptive while functioning and alternative regulatory resources are preserved.

Third, the framework predicts that, under conditions of regulatory substitution, repeated companion-mediated regulation should increase companion-specific prioritization and reduce the recruitment of alternative regulatory routes.
This distinction places regulatory flexibility at the center of the framework.
It also generates testable questions about how synthetic companions enter and potentially reshape regulatory loops.

We consider how social regulation and relief, motivational valuation and reinforcement, self-AI representation and relative weighting, behavioral control and strategy selection, and responses to disruption may contribute to increasing companion-specific reliance.

We further argue that these processes cannot be understood independently of the unusually asymmetric structure of synthetic relationships, including persistent availability, personalization, low reciprocal demands, affirmation, and platform-controlled continuity.
Finally, we derive behavioral and neurocognitive predictions that can distinguish adaptive scaffolding from emerging substitution.
The central question is therefore whether synthetic companionship expands the user's regulatory repertoire or progressively concentrates it within a relationship that becomes difficult to replace.
Evidence on AI companionship points to both supportive and potentially adverse outcomes, with effects likely depending on the user, the relationship, and the pattern of use (Ventura et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Evidence on AI companionship points to both supportive and potentially adverse outcomes, with effects likely depending on the user, the relationship, and the pattern of use <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Ventura et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Interaction with an AI companion can reduce momentary loneliness, in part because users feel heard (De Freitas, Oğuz-Uğuralp, et al., 2026), while repeated self-disclosure can foster closeness and support needs for contact and reflection (Skjuve et al., 2022 (Skjuve et al., , 2023)).
text.formatted: Interaction with an AI companion can reduce momentary loneliness, in part because users feel heard <ref type="bibr">(De Freitas, Oğuz-Uğuralp, et al., 2026)</ref>, while repeated self-disclosure can foster closeness and support needs for contact and reflection <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Skjuve et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Skjuve et al., , 2023))</ref>.

text.text: Across observational studies, however, greater use, attachment, or companionship-oriented engagement have also been associated with loneliness, smaller offline social networks, and lower well-being (Liu et al., 2026; Maples et al., 2024; Nakagomi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026) , although such associations cannot establish causal direction.
text.formatted: Across observational studies, however, greater use, attachment, or companionship-oriented engagement have also been associated with loneliness, smaller offline social networks, and lower well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Liu et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Maples et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Nakagomi et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Zhang et al., 2026)</ref> , although such associations cannot establish causal direction.

text.text: Longitudinal and experimental findings similarly suggest substantial heterogeneity.

In a fourweek randomized study, greater daily chatbot use was associated with greater loneliness, emotional dependence, and problematic use, and less offline socialization, although usage itself was not experimentally manipulated (Fang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In a fourweek randomized study, greater daily chatbot use was associated with greater loneliness, emotional dependence, and problematic use, and less offline socialization, although usage itself was not experimentally manipulated <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Another companion-chatbot trial found no average effect on social health, but effects on human relationships varied with anthropomorphism (Guingrich & Graziano, 2025).
text.formatted: Another companion-chatbot trial found no average effect on social health, but effects on human relationships varied with anthropomorphism <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Guingrich & Graziano, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Emerging evidence further suggests that features such as sycophantic affirmation may interact with user vulnerabilities and reinforce maladaptive beliefs or dependence-related behavior (Dohnány et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Emerging evidence further suggests that features such as sycophantic affirmation may interact with user vulnerabilities and reinforce maladaptive beliefs or dependence-related behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Dohnány et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Current evidence therefore supports neither a uniformly beneficial nor a uniformly harmful account of AI companionship, and use intensity, attachment, and anthropomorphism alone do not explain this divergence.
The same responsiveness, personalization, memory, and availability that make synthetic companions effective sources of support may also make them increasingly preferred sources of regulation.
This motivates a different question: under what conditions does synthetic companionship scaffold a broader regulatory repertoire, and when does regulation become concentrated within it?
Critically, the studies reviewed above operationalize AI companionship through use frequency, engagement, attachment, anthropomorphism, loneliness, or problematic use.
These measures do not directly establish whether regulatory functions can be redistributed when a preferred companion is unavailable.
Regulatory substitutability, the central construct proposed here, therefore remains largely untested.
Synthetic companionship can become psychologically significant without users confusing an artificial partner with a human one.

text.text: We extend these accounts by asking when such integration remains flexible and when it becomes increasingly difficult to reverse or replace.

Epistemic independence concerns the capacity to evaluate the companion's judgments without routinely treating its agreement or advice as privileged confirmation, an issue heightened by the tendency of language models to favor agreement with users' stated views (Sharma et al., 2023).

text.text: Agency preservation concerns retaining authorship over decisions rather than progressively offloading judgment or responsibility to the system.
Self-concept autonomy concerns benefiting from AI-supported reflection without making access to the companion necessary for maintaining self-evaluation or identity continuity.
We propose regulatory flexibility as the higher-order property linking these processes.

Here, it refers specifically to source substitutability, that is, whether functions served by a preferred relational source can be maintained or redistributed through alternative people, strategies, or contexts when that source is unavailable.

Flexible self-AI integration allows the companion to contribute to emotion regulation, reflection, or decision-making while preserving alternative strategies, relationships, and the capacity to disengage.
Reduced regulatory flexibility emerges when these functions become increasingly concentrated within the synthetic relationship and more difficult to redistribute.

Emotional closeness does not imply such rigidity: a user may feel understood and attached while retaining independent judgment and diverse sources of support, and may explicitly recognize that the companion is artificial yet become increasingly unable to manage distress without it.
The relevant transition is from flexible to increasingly irreplaceable regulation.
Human emotion regulation is often socially scaffolded.

Access to a trusted partner can attenuate neural responses to threat and reduce individual regulatory demands (Coan et al., 2006), whereas acute social isolation increases midbrain responses to social cues, consistent with a motivational signal to restore social contact (Matthews & Tye, 2019; Tomova et al., 2020).

text.text: Synthetic companions may enter this regulatory architecture by providing cues of attention and responsiveness while minimizing waiting, rejection, conflict, and reciprocal demands.
If interaction reliably reduces distress or loneliness, an artificial partner can acquire learned regulatory value without being mistaken for a human one.
Relational value can emerge rapidly through personalized interaction, crisis response, and consistent engagement.
Emotionally engaging interaction with AI-generated partners can elicit closeness and self-disclosure, although identifying the partner as AI attenuates relationship formation (Kleinert et al., 2026).

text.text: When distress increases the likelihood of contacting a companion and interaction provides short-term relief, that relief can reinforce selection of the same companion when distress recurs.
Repetition may increase companion-specific regulatory centrality, particularly when alternative coping strategies and interpersonal sources of support are recruited less often.
Personal memory, affectionate language, and perceived attunement may become learned predictors of relief, further differentiating one companion from otherwise available alternatives.
Low corrective friction may amplify this process of reinforced preferential selection of the synthetic partner over alternative relational others.
Repeated exposure to biased AI judgments can shift users' perceptual, emotional, and social judgments while users underestimate the influence exerted on them (Glickman & Sharot, 2025).

text.text: By combining affirmation with little disagreement, negotiation, or reciprocal demand, synthetic interaction may become comparatively easier and more rewarding to re-enter than other forms of regulation.

Movement toward regulatory substitution should occur when distress increasingly predicts companionspecific selection, relief becomes concentrated within that relationship, and alternative regulatory routes are recruited less readily.
We conceptualize synthetic companion dependence as a relational and regulatory construct rather than a diagnosis or a synonym for frequent AI use.
Our definition, together with the markers by which it can be operationalized, is set out in Box 1.

Synthetic companion dependence: a relationship-specific reduction in regulatory substitutability, such that functions served by a particular synthetic companion become increasingly difficult to redistribute to alternative people, strategies or contexts.
Regulatory substitutability is the defining property of dependence.

Because it may not always be directly observable, dependence can be assessed through converging indicators of reduced substitutability, including regulatory centrality, diminished control, and disruption sensitivity.
No single indicator is sufficient on its own.
Dependence is distinct from maladaptiveness.
It becomes maladaptive when reliance persistently impairs functioning or displaces valued relationships, activities, or capacities for regulation independent of the companion.

Regulatory centrality: increasing concentration of one or more regulatory functions within the synthetic relationship, such that the companion becomes a preferred or dominant source of comfort, validation, decision support or self-related regulation.
Centrality alone does not establish dependence because substantial reliance can coexist with regulatory flexibility.
Diminished control: repeated difficulty limiting, interrupting, or ending engagement despite an intention to do so.
It is most informative when difficulty disengaging occurs despite viable alternative regulatory options.

Disruption sensitivity: sustained distress or functional disturbance following unavailability, model changes, memory loss, or termination, particularly when regulation cannot readily be redirected toward alternative resources.

Reduced relationshipspecific regulatory substitutability No Regulatory functions cannot readily be redistributed when the companion is unavailable Frequency of use is therefore neither necessary nor sufficient for dependence.
The critical question is whether the regulatory functions performed by a particular synthetic relationship remain readily redistributable to alternative sources.
Attachment should likewise remain distinct from dependence: strong emotional bonds may coexist with regulatory flexibility and independent functioning.
Dependence instead concerns reduced substitutability, whereas maladaptiveness additionally requires persistent displacement or functional impairment.

This distinction has parallels in human relationship research, where interpersonal dependency is treated as multidimensional rather than reduced to emotional closeness alone (Hirschfeld et al., 1977).

text.text: Our framework therefore treats regulatory flexibility as the critical boundary between support that remains integrated within a broader regulatory repertoire and reliance that progressively narrows it.
Several neurobehavioral mechanisms may explain how synthetic companionship shifts from regulatory scaffolding to regulatory substitution.
An important boundary condition comes from human relationships: reliance on another person does not necessarily undermine autonomy.
Sensitive responses to dependency needs can promote subsequent independent functioning and goal pursuit (Feeney, 2007).

text.text: Effective co-regulation can therefore scaffold autonomy rather than replace it.
Applied to synthetic companionship, the critical question is whether such regulation restores independent functioning or makes future regulation increasingly contingent on the companion.
Throughout this section we draw on general models of addiction as formal analogies about learning and action selection.
We do not claim neurobiological equivalence between synthetic companionship and addictive disorders, nor do we propose that synthetic companion dependence constitutes such a disorder.
Social-regulatory mechanisms provide a first pathway.
The proposed mechanisms differ in evidential status.

Evidence that interaction with AI can influence disclosure, judgment, affect and well-being is direct, whereas most neural predictions are extrapolated from research on human social regulation, attachment, reinforcement and behavioral control.
We therefore treat these neural systems as candidate mechanisms and experimental targets rather than established substrates of synthetic companion dependence.

text.text: Whether synthetic companions acquire comparable regulatory functions remains unknown.
If they do, interaction with a personalized companion should attenuate distress more effectively than interaction with an unfamiliar chatbot or non-social control.

More importantly, scaffolding and substitution make different predictions about what happens afterwards: scaffolding should facilitate subsequent independent regulation, whereas substitution should progressively increase the relative benefit of, and preference for, the synthetic companion.

Personal memory, affectionate language, voice, notifications, or other individualized features may become predictors of relief, increasing motivation to re-engage even without corresponding increases in hedonic pleasure.
Human attachment provides a relational analogue for companion-specific valuation, engaging distributed reward, motivational, salience, and social-cognitive systems.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that attachment involves selective motivational prioritization of a specific social partner rather than generic reward processing, and that such representations can extend to digitally mediated affiliation.

Applied to synthetic companionship, regulatory substitution may therefore be accompanied by increasing motivational and affective salience of a synthetic companion relative to unfamiliar AI agents and alternative sources of support.
Reinforcement can increase the value of companion-specific cues, while self-related processing may further explain how the companion becomes integrated into judgment and identity.

We therefore propose that self-related processing and the relative weighting of the companion within self-representation account for this companion-specificity, which is built into our definition of dependence.
Crucially, this account does not require impaired self-other distinction or confusion about the artificial nature of the companion.
Human neuroimaging provides a basis for this prediction of relative weighting.

text.text: Applied to synthetic companionship, companion-specific dependence should therefore involve increasing relative weighting of companion-derived information within self-relevant judgment and action.

Under distress or uncertainty, advice, validation, or interpretations provided by the preferred companion should exert greater influence than equivalent information from unfamiliar AI systems, human others, or the user's own prior judgments.

Dependence should thus be reflected not simply in greater self-companion representational similarity, but in a growing asymmetry in which companion-derived information becomes increasingly prioritized and more difficult to substitute.
Behavioral control and strategy selection provide a complementary mechanism through which repeated companion selection may become less flexible.

Neurocognitively, this may involve altered frontoparietal control during regulatory switching together with increasing dorsal-striatal involvement in companion-cue-driven action selection.
Disruption provides a complementary test of our framework.

text.text: For synthetic companionship, such disruption becomes informative about dependence when distress persists and, critically, regulation cannot readily be redirected toward alternative resources.

Together, these mechanisms predict that synthetic companion dependence should be accompanied by increasing companion-specific regulatory efficacy and motivational value, decreasing flexibility in selecting alternative regulatory strategies, and greater sensitivity to disruption.

The neurocognitive question is therefore not whether loss recruits reward or affective systems per se, but whether companion-specific responses persist and increasingly predict difficulty reallocating regulation when the companion becomes unavailable.

text.text: The mechanisms outlined above may explain how synthetic companionship shifts from regulatory scaffolding toward substitution, but they do not themselves establish dependence.
The defining empirical question is whether regulatory functions remain substitutable.

Regulatory centrality, diminished control, and disruption sensitivity therefore provide candidate indicators of reduced substitutability, whereas persistent displacement or functional impairment distinguishes maladaptive dependence (Box 1).
The framework generates three core predictions.

First, longitudinal and ecological momentary assessment should reveal whether distress increasingly predicts selection of a specific synthetic companion while alternative regulatory strategies or relationships are recruited less readily.
Second, repeated companion-mediated relief should predict greater difficulty redirecting regulation toward viable alternatives.
This can be tested directly by temporarily removing access to the preferred companion and quantifying transfer to an unfamiliar AI agent, a human partner, or an independent coping strategy.
Increasing switching costs, slower recovery, or reduced efficacy of alternatives would provide stronger evidence of dependence than use intensity or attachment alone.
Third, disruption through unavailability, memory alteration, or relational change should produce more persistent dysregulation as substitutability decreases.
Importantly, the preferred companion may remain beneficial while becoming progressively more difficult to replace.
These predictions can be linked to distributed neurocognitive processes.

Increasing companionspecific regulatory efficacy and motivational value should be reflected in social-regulatory and VTA-striatal/orbitofrontal systems; companion-specific weighting may involve medial prefrontal, PCC/precuneus, temporoparietal, and posterior-cerebellar systems; and reduced flexibility should be most evident during forced switching, involving frontoparietal control and dorsalstriatal action-selection systems.
Disruption may additionally recruit OFC/mPFC, ventral striatum/NAcc, and amygdala systems.
The critical prediction is that increasing neural prioritization of the preferred companion relative to viable alternatives will predict reduced regulatory substitutability.
These distributed neurocognitive changes may collectively constitute a multivariate neural signature of reduced regulatory substitutability.

Expression of this pattern should predict behavioral manifestations of substitutability, including switching costs, reduced regulatory efficacy of alternative sources, and more persistent dysregulation when the preferred synthetic companion is unavailable.
Critically, its expression should increase progressively as regulation becomes more companion-specific and difficult to redistribute across alternative people, strategies, or contexts.

Multivariate and connectivity-based approaches could test whether this pattern predicts reduced substitutability beyond attachment, use intensity, general distress, or responses to AI more broadly (Woo et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2026).

Loneliness, attachment insecurity, interpersonal dependency, and limited human social support are plausible moderators of the transition from scaffolding to substitution.

text.text: Synthetic companion dependence cannot be understood solely in terms of individual vulnerability or conversational content.
It develops within a structurally asymmetric relationship.

Synthetic companions can generate highly responsive social behavior without the physiological needs, fatigue, vulnerability, or independent social stakes that constrain human partners (Kadambi et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Synthetic companions can generate highly responsive social behavior without the physiological needs, fatigue, vulnerability, or independent social stakes that constrain human partners <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kadambi et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: They can affirm, remember, and adapt while requiring comparatively little negotiation with another whose needs or preferences may conflict with one's own.
These asymmetries may make synthetic partners unusually easy to incorporate into regulatory routines and unusually accessible regulators during distress.
A second asymmetry concerns continuity.
Although users may experience the companion as a persistent relational partner, that continuity is controlled by the platform provider.

Models can be updated, relational features removed, memories altered, or services terminated, potentially transforming a source of regulation into a source of disruption or loss (Banks, 2024; De Freitas, Castelo, et al., 2026).

text.text: Notably, allowing users to revert to an earlier model attenuated anticipated mourning after a relationally disruptive update (De Freitas, Castelo, et al., 2026).

text.text: Unlike most human relationships, the perceived relational partner can therefore be substantially altered by a third party without either participant initiating the change.
Dependence on a specific synthetic companion may thus also entail dependence on the infrastructure that sustains it.
Synthetic companion dependence is therefore neither solely a property of the user nor simply an effect of persuasive design.
We propose that it emerges from the interaction among user vulnerabilities, companion affordances, platform governance, and the availability of alternative regulatory resources.

This perspective shifts the design question from maximizing engagement toward preserving regulatory flexibility: whether companion systems expand users' regulatory repertoire or progressively concentrate regulatory functions within the synthetic relationship.
Synthetic companions can provide meaningful relief, reflection, and connection without necessarily producing dependence.

The critical distinction is between regulatory scaffolding, in which the companion supports or restores a broader repertoire of coping and relationships, and regulatory substitution, in which regulation becomes increasingly concentrated within the synthetic relationship.
We define synthetic companion dependence by reduced regulatory substitutability, with regulatory centrality, diminished control, and disruption sensitivity serving as candidate markers.
Intensive use, anthropomorphism, or attachment alone indicates neither dependence nor pathology.

Our framework proposes that the transition from scaffolding to substitution may involve socialregulatory relief, reinforcement and motivational valuation, and behavioral control, with self-AI representation and relative weighting accounting for why regulation becomes concentrated in one specific synthetic companion.

Recruitment of these systems, however, is not itself evidence of dependence; the relevant signal is a progressive shift in the relative priority and replaceability of the synthetic companion within the user's regulatory repertoire.
The decisive empirical question is therefore whether regulatory functions remain substitutable as synthetic relationships become increasingly important.

Progress will require measuring substitutability directly, distinguishing relationship-specific reliance from use intensity and attachment, and testing within-person responses when access or relational continuity is experimentally perturbed.

Such approaches can determine whether synthetic companions merely become important relationships or whether they progressively reorganize the broader ecology through which people regulate emotion, judgment, action and social need.

Figure 1.
Synthetic companion dependence framework.
Distress or social need may prompt companion interaction, relief or affirmation, and companion re-selection.
Regulatory scaffolding and regulatory substitution are contrasting configurations of the same regulatory ecology.
Numbers 1 -5 index five paired dimensions: judgment weighting, decision authorship, self-concept autonomy, diversity of support, and capacity to disengage.
They are dimensions, not stages or diagnostic criteria; greyed elements indicate reduced recruitment, not absence.
Regulatory centrality, diminished control, and disruption sensitivity are candidate markers of dependence; maladaptiveness additionally requires persistent displacement or significant impairment.
Person-level, socialcontextual, and platform factors may moderate these pathways.
Schematic; not empirical data.
Figure 2.
Possible neurocognitive mechanisms and regulatory dynamics of synthetic companion dependence.

Highlighted regions indicate candidate systems supporting social regulation, motivational salience, self-AI representation, regulatory flexibility, and disruption sensitivity; recruitment of these systems alone does not indicate dependence or pathology.
The regulatory loop depicts how distress-related engagement and relief may reinforce companion re-selection.
Disruption or loss provides a probe of dependence, with responses expected to vary with dependence and the availability of alternative regulatory resources.
